title: Job's Hand over His Mouth, and Behemoth
summary: God challenges Job to answer, and Job replies that he is insignificant and will say no more. God speaks again from the whirlwind, asking whether Job would condemn God to justify himself, and invites him to put on majesty and humble every proud man if he can. Then God points to Behemoth, a massive creature he made along with Job, which lies among the reeds, unafraid of the raging river, and which no one can capture.
story: God's first speech (chapters 38 and 39) ended with the eagle on its crag. Now God pauses and calls for Job's response. Job, who through chapter after chapter had demanded a hearing and declared he would approach God like a prince (31:37), now lays his hand over his mouth. But God is not finished. His second speech (40:6 to 41:34) moves from Job's words to Job's stance: in defending his own innocence, Job has come close to putting God in the wrong. God then describes two great creatures, Behemoth in this chapter and Leviathan in the next, before Job's final reply in chapter 42.
historical:
Like the rest of God's speeches, this chapter belongs to the book's patriarchal setting and reflects the natural world known to the ancient Near East. The creature named Behemoth is the subject of long discussion. The name is the plural form of the ordinary Hebrew word for beast, probably meaning the beast of beasts, the supreme animal. Many scholars identify it with the hippopotamus: it eats grass, lies in marshes among reeds and lotus, is at home in rushing water, and was famously difficult to kill. Hippopotamuses lived in the Nile, and Egyptian art shows kings and nobles hunting them from boats with harpoons, sometimes as a symbol of subduing disorder. Others have suggested the elephant or the water buffalo.

The mention of the Jordan (verse 23) doesn't necessarily mean the animal lived there; it may be a poetic way of naming any mighty, surging river. Some interpreters, noting the creature's exaggerated features (bones like bronze, a tail like a cedar), think it is a real animal described in heightened, mythic language, like the Leviathan of chapter 41. Some modern readers, especially young-earth creationists, have proposed that Behemoth was a dinosaur, pointing to the tail compared to a cedar; most scholars read that line as describing the hippo's short tail poetically or as referring to another body part.
cultural:
God's challenge in verses 10 to 14 draws on the imagery of kingship in the ancient world. Kings were clothed in majesty and splendor, and one of their central duties was to bring down the proud and punish the wicked. God invites Job to take up this royal role over the whole world: if Job can humble every proud person and bury the wicked in the dust, then God will concede that Job's own right hand can save him. The right hand was the symbol of strength and effective action. The point is that justice across all creation is God's work, not Job's.

Job's gesture in verse 4, placing his hand over his mouth, was a recognized sign of silence and respect before someone greater. Earlier in the book Job described young men and princes doing just this when he entered the city gate (29:9). Now he does it before God. In an honor culture, it marks a decisive shift: Job stops pressing his case.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 5 are a short exchange between God's first and second speeches: God's challenge and Job's first response, in which he says he has spoken once, even twice, and will add nothing. Verses 6 to 14 open the second speech with the same formula as the first (brace yourself like a man) and then a series of pointed questions about justice and power. Verses 15 to 24 begin the portrait of Behemoth, arranged as a description of the body (verses 15 to 19), its habitat (20 to 23), and a closing question about capture (24). The movement from God's challenge to Job, to a creature only God can master, is deliberate: Behemoth is an example of power beyond Job's reach.

outline.t: God calls on the faultfinder to answer
Job lays his hand over his mouth
Would you condemn me to justify yourself?
Behemoth, the foremost of God's works
Behemoth in the marsh, beyond human capture

doctrines.note: God alone has the arm and voice to rule the world, humble the proud, and judge the wicked. Behemoth, the foremost of his works, can be approached only by its Maker. God's sovereignty is displayed both in governing human justice and in mastering the most powerful creatures.

God asks whether Job would annul his justice. Judging the proud and the wicked across all creation is God's prerogative, which he does not share with any creature. Job's case is real, but the verdict belongs to God.

Behemoth is a creature God made along with Job. Human beings stand among the creatures, not above creation as its masters. Job's recognition that he is insignificant is not self-hatred but a true sense of his place.

words.note: Behemoth, the plural of the common word for beast or cattle, used here for a single creature. The plural likely intensifies the meaning: the beast par excellence. The word has become a byword in English for anything huge. God calls it the foremost of his works (verse 19), language that echoes the description of wisdom as the first of God's ways in Proverbs 8:22.

Mishpat, justice or judgment, the word that has run through the whole debate. Job had complained that God denied him mishpat, and Elihu insisted that God does not pervert it. Now God asks whether Job would annul his mishpat, break or cancel God's own justice, in order to be declared right himself.

Tsadaq, to be righteous or to be in the right, often in a legal sense of being declared innocent. In verse 8 God asks whether Job would condemn God so that Job may be in the right. The question goes to the heart of the book: Job was right to insist on his innocence, but wrong to imply that God must therefore be guilty.

Yissor, faultfinder, found only here. It describes someone who corrects or reproves another, and here the faultfinder is Job, who has been correcting God. God's challenge in verse 2 uses it with gentle irony: will the one who corrects the Almighty now answer?

christ: God challenges Job to clothe himself with majesty, humble the proud, and save himself with his own right hand. Job cannot, and no human can. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who does what God describes, but in an unexpected way. Paul says that Christ, though in the form of God, humbled himself, and that God therefore highly exalted him (Philippians 2:6-11). Mary's song praises God for bringing down the proud and lifting up the humble (Luke 1:51-52). In Christ the right hand that saves is God's own, extended through a man. This is a thematic connection drawn from the whole biblical story, not a prediction in this chapter, but it answers the question God puts to Job: who can do this? God can, and in Christ he has.

hard.q: Is God rebuking Job for protesting his suffering?
hard.a:
In part, yes, but the rebuke is carefully limited. God's question in verse 8, would you condemn Me to justify yourself, identifies what went wrong in Job's speeches: in insisting that he was innocent, Job had drifted toward accusing God of injustice. God does not say Job was guilty of the sins the friends alleged, and he never retracts the prologue's verdict that Job was blameless. In chapter 42 God will say that Job spoke rightly of him, in contrast to the friends.

Interpreters reconcile these in different ways. Some say God rebukes Job's tone and overreach while approving his honesty. Others say God approves Job's refusal to accept false explanations, while correcting his demand that God answer to him. Either way, the book suggests that honest protest to God is not sin, but that it can cross into presuming to judge God. Job's response, silence and later repentance, is not a confession of the friends' charges but a recognition of who God is.

questions: Job had prepared to approach God like a prince, but when God speaks he lays his hand over his mouth. What changes in us when we move from talking about God to standing before him?
God asks, “Would you condemn Me to justify yourself?” In what ways do people defend themselves by blaming God, and how can honest complaint avoid that?
God points to Behemoth as a creature only its Maker can approach. What in your life reminds you that some things are beyond your control and belong to God?
